newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico debt payment raises transparency issue.
newsitem.headline: Mexico debt payment raises transparency issue.

text.p: Some observers of Mexico's finances are raising questions about the handling of a "special fund" that Mexico used to clear its debt to the U.S. Treasury and pay off some of what it owes to the International Monetary Fund.

Economists and Mexican newspaper columnists say the government should have made clear the fund existed before the prepayment was made in mid-January. While not criticizing the fact the payment was made, some economists say they will heighten their surveillance of the flows of government cash.
"I think they should have made it more transparent," said Lehamn Brothers economist John Welch.
"These specialized funds are good things to know about. Not only from a narrow-minded political sense...At the Federal Reserve you have to publish all your data."

The Mexican government made a splash in mid-January by paying $3.5 billion to the United States and $1.5 billion of its debt to the International Monetary Fund. Those were part of the foreign funds used to help bail Mexico out of its 1994-1995 financial crisis. Mexico's financial markets rallied sharply on the news of the paybacks.

The government said the funds to make the payments came from a mixture of recent bond and medium-term note issues, funds freed by the cancellation of Brady bonds, $550 million from state-owned oil company Pemex and $395 million from "other operations" in international capital markets.

The federal government made a point of saying the funds for the repayments did not come from international reserves, but were placed in a special fund that had been set up to house the cash. Observers question how appropriate it was for the funds to be kept off the books, saying they should have been recorded in the nation's international reserves.
"How is it that the funds for the payment were not registered in the country's international reserves," wrote Reforma newspaper in its widely-watched Templo Mayor column.
"Who had control of these funds and who received accounts during the time they were being 'guarded?'"

A spokesman for Banco de Mexico said the funds used to repay the U.S. Treasury at no time should have been part of the international reserves, as they were assets of the federal government. As far as the funds that were paid back to the IMF, they were recorded as a rise in net international assets, causing an increase of $1.5 billion after payment was made.

Analysts at Banamex issued a report last week that criticized the existence of the fund, saying the government should act with caution so as not to damage the credibility of the government's monetary program.
Mexico City newspapers ran the story, but Banamex then pulled back under what market sources described as pressure from the Finance Ministry.

On Monday, Banamex sent out a contrite news release saying its analysts believed "it is understandable that, given the imminence of the prepayment, a separate fund was set up at the central bank, before the transaction was made.
"Moreover...Banco de Mexico said the special fund for the prepayment was liquidated at the same moment it was used."
The issue took a political turn this week as well when opposition deputies in Congress said they wanted the finance minister to appear before them to explain the prepayment.
Economists said, moreover, that they will be much more careful watching where the government now places the funds it receives from issuing bonds.
"One can say that, because of this, we are going to take much more care in seeing where they are putting the flows of cash from placements...," Santander Investment economist Hector Chavez said.
Finance Ministry officials were not available for comment despite repeated calls.
